history.heading: Settlement
paragraphs: Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island, was one of the last major landmasses settled by humans. Austronesian seafarers from Borneo arrived perhaps 1,500 years ago, later joined by Bantu-speaking people from East Africa. Their mixed heritage shapes Malagasy language and culture today, along with Arab and later other influences.

history.heading: The Merina Kingdom
paragraphs: Various kingdoms developed, such as the Sakalava in the west. In the late 18th century, King Andrianampoinimerina unified the Merina of the central highlands, and his son Radama I extended control over much of the island. Protestant missionaries arrived and created a written Malagasy language. Queen Ranavalona I resisted European influence and persecuted Christians.

history.heading: French colony and independence
paragraphs: France conquered Madagascar in 1895–96 and abolished the monarchy. A nationalist uprising in 1947–48 was brutally crushed, with tens of thousands of deaths. Madagascar became independent on 26 June 1960.

Since independence, it has experienced periods of socialism, political crises and coups, notably in 2009. In October 2025, youth-led protests over water and power cuts led to President Andry Rajoelina's removal, after which a military-backed leader took power.

culture.heading: Malagasy traditions
paragraphs: Malagasy, an Austronesian language, and French are official. Traditional beliefs in ancestors coexist with Christianity, and in the famadihana ("turning of the bones") ceremony, families rewrap the remains of ancestors in fresh cloth. Fady (taboos) vary by region.
Rice is eaten at almost every meal. Hiragasy is a traditional performance combining music, dance and oratory. The valiha, a tube zither, is the national instrument.

culture.heading: Unique nature
paragraphs: Madagascar split from other landmasses tens of millions of years ago, and about 90 percent of its wildlife is found nowhere else, including lemurs, chameleons and the baobab trees of the Avenue of the Baobabs. Deforestation threatens this biodiversity.

politics.heading: Political transition
paragraphs: Madagascar is formally a semi-presidential republic, but its politics have been marked by repeated crises and unconstitutional changes of power. After the October 2025 events, Colonel Michael Randrianirina was sworn in as president and promised a transition toward new elections.

economy.heading: Vanilla and poverty
paragraphs: Madagascar is one of the world's poorest countries. It is the world's largest producer of vanilla and exports cloves, nickel, cobalt, ilmenite and textiles. Most people depend on subsistence farming.
Cyclones, droughts in the south causing famine, poor infrastructure and political instability hinder development. The currency is the ariary.
